prompt:
At Monday's practice, Lonnie sprints 200 m a total of 24 times. At Tuesday's practice, he sprints 240 m a total of 20 times. On both days, he rests for 30 s between each consecutive pair of sprints. Lonnie sprints at a constant speed of 8 m/s.

(a) On Monday, how many times does Lonnie take the 30 s rest between consecutive pairs of sprints?

solutions.title: Count the gaps
solutions.body:
Lonnie rests between sprints 1 and 2, between sprints 2 and 3, ..., and between sprints 23 and 24. That is one rest for each gap between consecutive sprints, and 24 sprints have $24 - 1 = 23$ gaps.

**Answer: 23**

solutions.title: Smaller case
solutions.body:
With 2 sprints there is 1 rest; with 3 sprints there are 2 rests. In general there is one rest fewer than the number of sprints, so 24 sprints give 23 rests.

**Answer: 23**

prompt:
At Monday's practice, Lonnie sprints 200 m a total of 24 times. At Tuesday's practice, he sprints 240 m a total of 20 times. On both days, he rests for 30 s between each consecutive pair of sprints. Lonnie sprints at a constant speed of 8 m/s.

(b) On Monday, determine Lonnie's total practice time. That is, determine the total number of seconds between the start of his first sprint and the end of his last sprint, including the rests.

solutions.title: Sprinting time plus resting time
solutions.body:
At 8 m/s, a 200 m sprint takes $\frac{200}{8} = 25$ s. The 24 sprints take $24 \times 25 = 600$ s.

From part (a) he rests 23 times for 30 s each: $23 \times 30 = 690$ s.

Total: $600 + 690 = 1290$ s.

**Answer: 1290 s**

solutions.title: Sprint-and-rest blocks
solutions.body:
Group each of the first 23 sprints with the rest that follows it: each block lasts $25 + 30 = 55$ s. Then add the last sprint alone: $23 \times 55 + 25 = 1265 + 25 = 1290$ s.

**Answer: 1290 s**

prompt:
At Monday's practice, Lonnie sprints 200 m a total of 24 times. At Tuesday's practice, he sprints 240 m a total of 20 times. On both days, he rests for 30 s between each consecutive pair of sprints. Lonnie sprints at a constant speed of 8 m/s.

(c) Determine how many fewer seconds Tuesday's practice will take compared to Monday's practice.

solutions.title: Compute Tuesday's practice
solutions.body:
Each 240 m sprint takes $\frac{240}{8} = 30$ s, so 20 sprints take $600$ s. There are 19 rests: $19 \times 30 = 570$ s. Tuesday's practice lasts $600 + 570 = 1170$ s.

Monday's practice lasted 1290 s (part (b)), so Tuesday's is $1290 - 1170 = 120$ s shorter.

**Answer: 120 seconds fewer**

solutions.title: Same distance, fewer rests
solutions.body:
Monday: $24 \times 200 = 4800$ m. Tuesday: $20 \times 240 = 4800$ m. Same distance at the same speed means the same sprinting time.

So the difference comes only from rests: 23 rests on Monday versus 19 on Tuesday, i.e. 4 fewer rests, saving $4 \times 30 = 120$ s.

**Answer: 120 seconds fewer**

prompt:
Consider the following arrangement of positive integers.

$$\begin{array}{cccc} 1 & & & \\ 2 & 4 & & \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & \\ 10 & 12 & 14 & 16 \\ \vdots & & & \end{array}$$

The 1st row includes the odd integer 1, and the 2nd row includes the two even integers 2 and 4. For $k \ge 2$, the $k$th row

- begins with the integer that is one more than the last integer in the previous row,
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive odd integers when $k$ is odd, and
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive even integers when $k$ is even.

A useful fact about this arrangement is that the integer in the $k$th row and $k$th position (that is, the last position in the $k$th row) is $k^2$. For example, $4^2 = 16$ and 16 is the integer in the 4th position of the 4th row.

(a) What is the average of the integers in the 5th row?

solutions.title: List the row
solutions.body:
Row 4 ends at 16, so row 5 starts at 17 and contains 5 consecutive odd integers: 17, 19, 21, 23, 25.

Average: $\frac{17+19+21+23+25}{5} = \frac{105}{5} = 21$.

**Answer: 21**

solutions.title: Middle term
solutions.body:
The integers in a row are equally spaced, so their average is the middle one. Row 5 is 17, 19, 21, 23, 25 and its middle entry is 21.

**Answer: 21**

The 1st row includes the odd integer 1, and the 2nd row includes the two even integers 2 and 4. For $k \ge 2$, the $k$th row

- begins with the integer that is one more than the last integer in the previous row,
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive odd integers when $k$ is odd, and
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive even integers when $k$ is even.

A useful fact about this arrangement is that the integer in the $k$th row and $k$th position (that is, the last position in the $k$th row) is $k^2$. For example, $4^2 = 16$ and 16 is the integer in the 4th position of the 4th row.

(b) Which row has the integer 145 in the 1st position?

solutions.title: Use the last entries
solutions.body:
The number in the first position of a row is one more than the last number of the previous row. Since $145 = 144 + 1$ and $144 = 12^2$ is the last entry of row 12, the integer 145 starts row 13.

**Answer: row 13**

solutions.title: First entries formula
solutions.body:
Row $k$ starts at $(k-1)^2 + 1$. Setting $(k-1)^2 + 1 = 145$ gives $(k-1)^2 = 144$, so $k - 1 = 12$ and $k = 13$.

**Answer: row 13**

Consider the following arrangement of positive integers.

$$\begin{array}{cccc} 1 & & & \\ 2 & 4 & & \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & \\ 10 & 12 & 14 & 16 \\ \vdots & & & \end{array}$$

The 1st row includes the odd integer 1, and the 2nd row includes the two even integers 2 and 4. For $k \ge 2$, the $k$th row

- begins with the integer that is one more than the last integer in the previous row,
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive odd integers when $k$ is odd, and
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive even integers when $k$ is even.

A useful fact about this arrangement is that the integer in the $k$th row and $k$th position (that is, the last position in the $k$th row) is $k^2$. For example, $4^2 = 16$ and 16 is the integer in the 4th position of the 4th row.

(c) Determine the row and the position in which the integer 1598 appears.

solutions.title: Work back from a perfect square
solutions.body:
Since $40^2 = 1600$, the integer 1600 is in the last (40th) position of row 40. Row 40 is an even row, so its entries are consecutive even integers, decreasing by 2 from right to left. Row 40 starts at $39^2 + 1 = 1522$, which is less than 1598, so 1598 is in row 40, and it is just before 1600: $1600 - 2 = 1598$ is in position 39.

**Answer: row 40, position 39**

solutions.title: Count from the start of the row
solutions.body:
Row 40 begins at $39^2 + 1 = 1522$ and goes up by 2. The entry in position $j$ is $1522 + 2(j-1)$. Setting $1522 + 2(j - 1) = 1598$ gives $2(j-1) = 76$, so $j = 39$.

**Answer: row 40, position 39**

prompt:
Consider the following arrangement of positive integers.

$$\begin{array}{cccc} 1 & & & \\ 2 & 4 & & \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & \\ 10 & 12 & 14 & 16 \\ \vdots & & & \end{array}$$

The 1st row includes the odd integer 1, and the 2nd row includes the two even integers 2 and 4. For $k \ge 2$, the $k$th row

- begins with the integer that is one more than the last integer in the previous row,
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive odd integers when $k$ is odd, and
- includes, in increasing order, $k$ consecutive even integers when $k$ is even.

A useful fact about this arrangement is that the integer in the $k$th row and $k$th position (that is, the last position in the $k$th row) is $k^2$. For example, $4^2 = 16$ and 16 is the integer in the 4th position of the 4th row.

(d) The average of the integers in row $r$ is 241. Determine the value of $r$.

solutions.title: Average of first and last
solutions.body:
The entries of a row increase by a constant 2, so the average of a row equals the average of its first and last entries.

Row 16 ends at $16^2 = 256$ and starts at $15^2 + 1 = 226$. Its average is $\frac{226 + 256}{2} = 241$. So $r = 16$.

**Answer: $r = 16$**

solutions.title: Squeeze between squares
solutions.body:
Every entry in rows 1 to 15 is at most $15^2 = 225$, so their averages are at most 225 < 241. Every entry in rows 17 and later is more than $16^2 = 256$, so their averages exceed 256 > 241. Hence $r = 16$. Check: row 16 is $226, 228, \ldots, 256$, with average $\frac{226+256}{2} = 241$. ✓

**Answer: $r = 16$**

solutions.title: Digit sum
solutions.body:
The digit sum is $4 + B + 5 + B + 2 = 2B + 11$. Trying $B = 1, \ldots, 9$ gives $13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29$; the multiples of 3 are $15, 21, 27$, which occur for $B = 2, 5, 8$.

**Answer: $B = 2, 5$ or $8$**

solutions.title: Remainders
solutions.body:
We need $2B + 11 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$, i.e. $2B \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, i.e. $B \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (since $2 \cdot 2 = 4 \equiv 1$). The non-zero digits with remainder 2 are 2, 5, 8.

**Answer: $B = 2, 5$ or $8$**

solutions.title: Restrict B first
solutions.body:
The digit sum is $3A + 2B$. Since $3A$ is a multiple of 3, the number is divisible by 3 exactly when $2B$ is, i.e. when $B = 3, 6, 9$. So $B \in \{1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8\}$.

Divisibility by 4 means the two-digit number $\overline{BA}$ is a multiple of 4:

| $B$ | $A$ with $\overline{BA}$ divisible by 4 |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2, 6 (12, 16) |
| 2 | 4, 8 (24, 28) |
| 4 | 4, 8 (44, 48) |
| 5 | 2, 6 (52, 56) |
| 7 | 2, 6 (72, 76) |
| 8 | 4, 8 (84, 88) |

That is $6 \times 2 = 12$ pairs.

**Answer: 12**

solutions.title: Restrict A first
solutions.body:
A multiple of 4 is even, so $A \in \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$. A two-digit number $\overline{BA}$ ending in 2 or 6 is a multiple of 4 exactly when $B$ is odd; ending in 4 or 8, exactly when $B$ is even. Removing $B = 3, 6, 9$ (which make the number divisible by 3):

- $A = 2$ or $6$: $B \in \{1, 5, 7\}$ — 3 choices each;
- $A = 4$ or $8$: $B \in \{2, 4, 8\}$ — 3 choices each.

Total $4 \times 3 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

solutions.title: Use 5, then 4, then 3
solutions.body:
**Divisible by 5.** $ACA2$ ends in 2, so it is not divisible by 5. Since 5 is prime, $BAC$ must be, so $C = 5$. Now $t = A5A2 \times BA5$.

**Not divisible by 12.** $t$ is divisible by 3, so it must not be divisible by 4. $BA5$ is odd, so all factors of 2 in $t$ come from $A5A2$; thus $A5A2$ must not be divisible by 4, i.e. $\overline{A2}$ is not a multiple of 4. The numbers $12, 32, 52, 72, 92$ are multiples of 4 and $22, 42, 62, 82$ are not, so $A \in \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$.

**Divisible by 3.** Since 3 is prime, $A5A2$ (digit sum $2A + 7$) or $BA5$ (digit sum $A + B + 5$) must be divisible by 3.

- $A = 2$: $2A + 7 = 11$, so need $B + 7 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$: $B = 2, 5, 8$ — 3 triples.
- $A = 4$: $2A + 7 = 15$ ✓, any $B$ — 9 triples.
- $A = 6$: $2A + 7 = 19$, need $B + 11 \equiv 0$: $B = 1, 4, 7$ — 3 triples.
- $A = 8$: $2A + 7 = 23$, need $B + 13 \equiv 0$: $B = 2, 5, 8$ — 3 triples.

Total $3 + 9 + 3 + 3 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

solutions.title: Count with remainders mod 3
solutions.body:
As above, $C = 5$ and $A \in \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$. Working mod 3, $A5A2 \equiv 2A + 1$ and $BA5 \equiv A + B + 2$.

$A5A2$ is a multiple of 3 iff $A \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, which among $\{2,4,6,8\}$ happens only for $A = 4$ (all 9 values of $B$ work).

For the other three values of $A$ we need $B \equiv -(A+2) \pmod 3$, and exactly 3 of the digits $1$–$9$ lie in each residue class mod 3, giving 3 choices of $B$ each.

Total $9 + 3 \cdot 3 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

prompt:
A lab has 50 computers numbered 1 through 50. Each pair of computers is connected to each other by a cord. The cords are coloured according to the following rules.

- If the numbers of the two computers are both even or both odd, then the cord connecting them is red.
- Otherwise, the cord connecting them is blue.

A *route* is a sequence of cords along which data can travel to get from one computer to another computer within the lab. For example, data could travel the route from Computer 5 to Computer 12 directly, or the route from Computer 5 to Computer 15 to Computer 12.

(a) There is a route connecting Computer 1 to Computer $n$ using only red cords. If $n \ne 1$, how many possible values are there for $n$?

solutions.title: Red cords keep parity
solutions.body:
Every red cord joins two computers of the same parity, so a route of red cords starting at the odd Computer 1 only ever reaches odd computers. Conversely, Computer 1 is joined to every other odd computer directly by a red cord. So the possible $n$ are the odd numbers $3, 5, \ldots, 49$: there are 24 of them.

**Answer: 24**

solutions.title: Count odd numbers
solutions.body:
There are 25 odd numbers from 1 to 50. Each odd computer can be reached from Computer 1 by one red cord, no even computer can be reached using red cords only, and $n \ne 1$ removes one: $25 - 1 = 24$.

**Answer: 24**

prompt:
A lab has 50 computers numbered 1 through 50. Each pair of computers is connected to each other by a cord. The cords are coloured according to the following rules.

- If the numbers of the two computers are both even or both odd, then the cord connecting them is red.
- Otherwise, the cord connecting them is blue.

A *route* is a sequence of cords along which data can travel to get from one computer to another computer within the lab. For example, data could travel the route from Computer 5 to Computer 12 directly, or the route from Computer 5 to Computer 15 to Computer 12.

(b) Show that for every pair of distinct computers, Computer $A$ and Computer $B$, there is always a route between them that uses only blue cords.
answer: If $A$, $B$ have different parity the cord $AB$ is blue; otherwise go through any computer $C$ of the other parity: $A 	o C 	o B$ uses two blue cords.

solutions.title: Two cases on parity
solutions.body:
**Different parity.** If one of $A$, $B$ is even and the other odd, the cord joining them directly is blue, so that single cord is a blue route.

**Same parity.** If $A$ and $B$ are both odd (or both even), choose any computer $C$ of the other parity (there are 25 of each, so such a $C$ exists). The cords $A$–$C$ and $C$–$B$ each join computers of different parity, so both are blue. The route $A \to C \to B$ uses only blue cords.

In every case there is a blue-only route. ∎

prompt:
A lab has 50 computers numbered 1 through 50. Each pair of computers is connected to each other by a cord. The cords are coloured according to the following rules.

- If the numbers of the two computers are both even or both odd, then the cord connecting them is red.
- Otherwise, the cord connecting them is blue.

A *route* is a sequence of cords along which data can travel to get from one computer to another computer within the lab. For example, data could travel the route from Computer 5 to Computer 12 directly, or the route from Computer 5 to Computer 15 to Computer 12.

(c) Each red cord and blue cord is removed and randomly replaced with either a green cord or a yellow cord. Dani notices that there is no route that connects Computer 1 to Computer 50 that uses only green cords. Show that there is always a route between Computer 13 and Computer 14 that uses only yellow cords.
answer: Cord 1–50 is yellow; for each of 13 and 14, one of its cords to 1 or to 50 is yellow (else a green route 1–x–50). Combining with the yellow cord 1–50 gives a yellow route 13 → 14.

solutions.title: Case analysis using the four cords
solutions.body:
If the cord 13–14 is yellow we are done, so suppose it is green.

There is no green route from 1 to 50, so:

- the cord 1–50 is yellow (otherwise it is a green route);
- the cord 1–13 or the cord 13–50 is yellow (otherwise $1 \to 13 \to 50$ is green);
- the cord 1–14 or the cord 14–50 is yellow (otherwise $1 \to 14 \to 50$ is green).

So Computer 13 has a yellow cord to 1 or to 50, and Computer 14 has a yellow cord to 1 or to 50. Four cases:

- 13–1 and 14–1 yellow: route $13 \to 1 \to 14$.
- 13–1 and 14–50 yellow: route $13 \to 1 \to 50 \to 14$.
- 13–50 and 14–1 yellow: route $13 \to 50 \to 1 \to 14$.
- 13–50 and 14–50 yellow: route $13 \to 50 \to 14$.

Each route uses only yellow cords. ∎

solutions.title: Yellow component containing 1 and 50
solutions.body:
Call a computer *joined* if it can reach Computer 1 by a yellow route. The cord 1–50 must be yellow (it is itself a route), so 50 is joined.

Take any other computer $x$. If both cords $x$–1 and $x$–50 were green, then $1 \to x \to 50$ would be a green route, which is impossible. So $x$ has a yellow cord to 1 or to 50, and since 1 and 50 are joined by a yellow cord, $x$ is joined.

Hence every computer, in particular 13 and 14, can reach Computer 1 by a yellow route; going from 13 to 1 and then from 1 to 14 gives a yellow route from 13 to 14 (a route may pass through any computers). ∎
